title: Wickliffe Mounds Mississippian village Ballard County
summary: Around 1100 CE, Mississippian farmers settled a bluff above the Mississippi–Ohio confluence in Ballard County and built a mound town that lasted until about 1350.
bodyMarkdown:
Around 1100 CE, Mississippian farmers settled on a bluff overlooking the meeting of the Mississippi and Ohio rivers, at today's Wickliffe in Ballard County. Their first village was compact, with houses clustered around an open plaza. Soon afterward, residents began raising two flat-topped platform mounds, now called Mounds A and B.

Most of the mound building happened between about 1175 and 1250. New households moved in, the community spread north and south, and the platform mounds grew in stages. A third mound, Mound C, later became a cemetery.

From 1250 to 1350 residents added four burial mounds, and the town reached the edge of the bluffs, covering about 7 acres. By 1350 they had capped the mounds and left.

On a hard clay house floor, archaeologists found a painted cross-and-circle, or Sun Circle: a cross on a white ground inside a red ochre ring. The symbol appears widely in Mississippian art, including on Wickliffe pottery. The site was dug as a 1930s tourist attraction called "Ancient Buried City," studied by Murray State University from the early 1980s, and joined Kentucky's state parks in 2004 as Wickliffe Mounds State Historic Site.

Source: [Kentucky Archaeological Survey, Wickliffe Mounds State Historic Site](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Wickliffe.aspx)
